passage:
'The cut-off for science is 85,' Kiran said, dropping onto the sofa. 'I got 79 in the pre-boards. It's over, Lokesh bhaiya.'
Lokesh muted the cricket. 'Is it? When are the actual boards?'
'March. But the paper setters, the checking, the cut-off, I can't control any of that.'
'True. So what can you touch today? Not March. Today.'
Kiran was quiet. 'I lost most marks in chemistry equations.'
'Okay. And?'
'I could do ten equations tonight. And ask Farida Ma'am tomorrow which ones I keep getting wrong.'
'That's today's thing. The cut-off is the cut-off.'
Kiran pulled the chemistry book out of the bag. 'And if I still don't make it?'
'Then you'll have done your part, and we'll look at the other streams together. Not your fault either way.'
'Ten equations,' Kiran said. 'Starting now.'

qa.q: What score did Kiran get in the pre-boards?
qa.a: 79 in the pre-boards, while the cut-off for science is 85.

qa.q: How was Kiran feeling when saying 'It's over'?
qa.a: Kiran felt hopeless, focusing only on the cut-off and the checking, which were out of Kiran's hands.

qa.q: What turning point moved Kiran from despair to action?
qa.a: Lokesh's question about what Kiran could touch today led Kiran to one step: ten equations tonight and asking Farida Ma'am which ones go wrong.

qa.q: How might Lokesh bhaiya see the role of an older brother in a moment like this?
qa.a: Lokesh seems to see the role as a steady helper who asks questions rather than lecturing, so Kiran finds the next step and keeps hope without self-blame.

grounding: Shows a teenager asking what can be done today, taking one action, and accepting that the cut-off itself cannot be changed.

passage:
When we moved from Lucknow to Nagpur last June, I spent the first three weeks in my room. 'Farhan, come and eat,' Ammi would call, and I'd say later. I couldn't change Abbu's transfer. I couldn't make my old friends live closer. Every night I scrolled through old photos and felt worse.
Then one evening I made a list on my phone: things I can do this week. It was short. Say hi to one person in class. Call Ayaan on Sunday. Find out if the school has a quiz club.
It did. That's where I met Aadhya, who argues about capital cities like her life depends on it. We came second at the inter-school round in October.
I still miss Lucknow. Some days a lot. But I stopped blaming myself for being lonely, and I stopped waiting for things to fix themselves.

qa.q: What was on the list of things to do that week?
qa.a: Say hi to one person in class, call Ayaan on Sunday, and find out if the school has a quiz club.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling in the first three weeks in Nagpur, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Farhan was sad and lonely; staying in the room, putting off meals and scrolling old photos every night show it.

qa.q: Which choice made the difference for Farhan, and why?
qa.a: Making a short list of small actions within reach, instead of wishing the transfer away, led to the quiz club and a new friend.

qa.q: How might Aadhya see Farhan, the newcomer at the quiz club?
qa.a: Aadhya likely sees a teammate who shares the love of quizzing, not someone lonely, since they came second together in October.

grounding: Shows a teenager who accepts a move they could not change, takes small actions within their control, and keeps hope without blaming themselves.
